I’m 47 years old and I’ve been farming my 8 mu of land in Quzhou County since I was a teenager. This year, like every year, I will grow winter wheat and summer maize in rotation on the same plots — it’s the only system that makes sense here on the North China Plain, and it’s what I know inside and out. I trust the wheat-maize double crop because the government sets a minimum purchase price for wheat, which guarantees my family’s income, and the maize gives me both cash from sales and grain for feeding pigs. I will plant 8 mu of improved wheat variety Luyuan 502 in late October. Before sowing, I will do rotary tillage to break up the maize stubble and prepare a good seedbed. I will apply about 100 jin of compound fertilizer (18-22-5) as basal dressing and topdress with urea at the jointing stage, which comes to about 36 kg nitrogen, 22 kg phosphorus, and 8 kg potassium per mu. I will irrigate four times — overwintering water, jointing, heading, and grain filling — using border irrigation from the village well. I will spray herbicide once after sowing, insecticide twice for aphids and armyworms, and fungicide once if powdery mildew appears, so about four pesticide applications in total. I expect a yield of around 1,000 kg per mu if the weather holds. Right after wheat harvest in early June, I will immediately sow 8 mu of hybrid maize Denghai 605 using no-tillage direct seeding, because the growing season is tight and I cannot afford to lose even five days. I will apply compound fertilizer (28-6-6) at sowing, totaling about 24 kg nitrogen, 6 kg phosphorus, and 6 kg potassium per mu. I will irrigate twice — at the jointing and big-trumpet stages — and spray herbicide once plus insecticide twice, making three pesticide applications. I expect about 1,100 kg per mu from the maize. This is my plan because it is proven, low-risk, and matches what the seed dealer, my neighbors, and my own experience tell me works best on this soil.
